entries.note: The course eaten after the table is 'disserved', or cleared of everything else; unrelated to [[desert]], but shares the verb 'serve' with [[just deserts]].
Means what you deserve; almost an eggcorn, since people assume it refers to [[dessert]], though both come from the same verb meaning to serve.
Comes from a different Latin root than [[dessert]], one meaning to join together or put in a row; a deserted place is cut off from humanity.
From tira 'pull', mi 'me', su 'up', so a pick-me-up, probably because of the coffee; a story about a Treviso brothel is doubted because the word isn't written down before the 1980s.
Word in the local Treviso dialect for a brothel madam, used in the tiramisu academy's aphrodisiac origin story for [[tiramisu]].
Possibly the basis of [[tiramisu]]; an Italian version of English trifle, with liqueur-soaked sponge layered with custard and fruit.
British name for what Americans call whipped cream; in Britain, whipped cream means liquid cream that has been whipped by hand.
A contraction of 'some more', first found as 'some mores' in a 1927 Girl Scouts cookbook; before it came marshmallow marguerites made on saltine crackers.

Named after Sylvester Graham, a Presbyterian minister and dietary reformer whose followers, the Grahamites, made coarse graham flour, bread and crackers; Britons and Americans pronounce Graham differently.
Short for the National Biscuit Company, which made the [[graham cracker]] what it is today and released the Mallomar in 1913.
Named not after Germany but after the English-American chocolate maker Samuel German, whose dark baking chocolate was used in the cake.
A chocolatey cake named after the Black Forest in Germany; its German name is Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte.
Not from German [[braten]] 'to roast', as many people assume; the 'brat' comes from a Middle High German term meaning diced meat.
A fat boiled sausage named not after the German word for goat but after [[bock]] beer, which it's served with in Berlin and Bavaria.
A seasonal dark lager, maybe named after goats because it makes you giddy, or after Einbeck, which sounds like 'ein Bock' in a Bavarian accent.
Wiener is German for 'from Vienna'; the sausage was invented in Frankfurt but loved in Vienna, where it's called a [[frankfurter]].
A small boiled sausage invented in Frankfurt that became so popular in Vienna that it got called a [[wiener]]; in Frankfurt, it's called a Vienna sausage.
German suffix showing where something comes from, found at the end of [[frankfurter]], [[wiener]] and [[hamburger]].
Literally a steak from Hamburg, formed with the German place suffix [[-er]].
Simply German for blood sausage.
A parboiled sausage named after German knacken 'to crackle', because it bursts; Americans often say 'knockwurst', which Rob calls wrong; it shares a Germanic root with [[knack]].
The English word, as in having the knack of something, which can also mean a snap, comes from the same Germanic root as [[knackwurst]].
Means something that has been cut, so its meaning is very close to [[cutlet]].
A word that one language lends to another and then gets back, like [[katsu]].
Short for katsuretsu, the Japanese version of English [[cutlet]] adapted to Japanese sound rules, which English then borrowed back as a [[boomerang word]].
An example of Japanese fitting an English word to its consonant-vowel pattern: beer becomes biru.
The Japanese version of English toilet, reshaped to follow the language's consonant-vowel sound pattern.
A Vietnamese noodle soup invented during French occupation; the name may come from French [[pot-au-feu]], from Chinese words like fàn, or from both.
A Sino-Korean word that has changed over time; the word it comes from literally means submerged vegetables.
A [[kimchi]] soup; jjigae just means soup.
A Korean rice dish, often served very hot in a stone bowl; its name sounds fun but just means mixed rice.
Korean beef dish whose name means fire meat, perhaps because it's slightly spicy.
Means stir-fried noodles; mein, mian or men in the name of an East Asian dish usually means noodles, as in [[lo mein]] and [[ramen]].
Means tossed noodles; like [[chow mein]], its name contains the word for noodles.
A Japanese version of a Chinese name meaning pulled noodles; the 'men' at the end means noodles, as in [[chow mein]].
Closer to the Mandarin gong bao, meaning palace guardian; thought to be named after the Qing Dynasty official Ding Baozhen, who loved the dish.
Its meaning is unknown and it's probably part of a longer phrase; theories include gratitude, 'barely fills your stomach' and 'so close to the heart'.
Hand-pulled noodles from Shaanxi, named for the sound of dough slapping the counter; biang is written with a single 58-stroke character, perhaps the most complex one in real use.
The word means the pounded rice paste mochi is made from; making it is called mochitsuki, and the product itself is shortened to mochi.
Literally means vinegar rice, so a dish without rice is technically not sushi.
Fresh fish served on its own, without the rice that makes a dish [[sushi]].
Means to grip or press with the hands, as the chef does to shape the rice under the fish, so it looks pressed in a palm.
From Latin [[tempora]] 'times', brought to Nagasaki by Portuguese Jesuits and referring to Ember days, when Catholics ate fish instead of meat; arguably a [[boomerang word]].
A Louisiana stew named after an African word for okra, possibly Bantu, from an unknown language; the dish mixes West African, French, Spanish, German and Choctaw influences.
A sassafras powder that the Choctaw contributed to [[gumbo]] as a thickener; the French term is related to [[filament]], meaning ropy or turned into threads.
Probably from the Provençal dish jambonetta, maybe linked to French [[jambe]] 'leg' or to giblets, and also to a French word for a mishmash; in 19th-century French it meant a raffle.
A Louisiana dish, usually made with crawfish, with sauce poured over it; the name just means smothered in French.
From Old French escrevis, reshaped to sound more English, which gave it a 'fish' ending although it isn't a fish; also called crawfish or crawdads.
Fried cornmeal balls, and to Rob a brand of shoe; the popular story says hunters fed them to dogs to keep them quiet, but the real origin is unknown.
Supposedly named after Jose Abeal Otero, a Havana bar owner nicknamed Sloppy Joe who created a ground-beef sandwich in 1917; Hemingway later got a Key West bar renamed Sloppy Joe's.
Named after the city of Bologna, like the cold meat [[bologna]].
The cold meat, pronounced 'baloney' in America, is spelled like the city of Bologna and named after it, like [[bolognese]].
Named after Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya, who made the dish up in 1943 at the Victory Club across the border from Texas and called it Nacho's special.
Probably a variant of [[pita]]; some Italian sources suggest a word meaning clamp, pound or stamp, perhaps because some pizzas are folded.
A Greek and Latin word for a piece of bread, from Greek peptos 'cooked'; the hosts aren't sure how to pronounce it.
Means a trouser leg or stocking, since it's stuffed like a foot in a sock; the same idea as French [[chausson]].
French for soft footwear or baby booties, and also a pastry; related to chaussette 'sock', chaussure 'shoe' and chaussée 'pavement', which all have to do with feet.
Means a sort of stick; a story says it was made to fit down soldiers' trouser legs, which is how Jess links it to [[calzone]].
One of several Italian pasta suffixes, along with -elli, -illi, -etti, -ine and -elle, that mean something small; the opposite of [[-oni]].
An Italian pasta suffix that, like -one and -otti, means something big; the opposite of [[-ini]].
An Italian suffix added to a pasta name when the pasta has been badly made, as in [[spaghettacci]].
Badly done [[spaghetti]] left in the water too long, formed with the suffix [[-acci]].
Literally means little strings.
Means little cut things; taglia is related to [[tailor]], since a tailor is ultimately just a cutter.
Pasta whose name means little bells.
Shell-shaped pasta whose name is like [[conch]]; Rob admits he mispronounced it for years by ignoring the Italian 'gl' sound.
Bow-tie pasta, whose Italian name means butterflies.
Means little tongues, apparently referring to snake tongues rather than human ones.
Doesn't mean 'little' anything; comes from the Italian verb [[pappare]], meaning to gobble something up.
Spiral pasta whose name means little spindles; discussed in an earlier episode on aeroplane parts alongside [[fuselage]], French for spindle.
Related to [[pen]]; it means a quill or feather, which the pasta looks like.
The more common, ridged type of [[penne]]; rigate means striped, and the ridges help the sauce cling.
Means smooth [[penne]], which doesn't have the ridges of [[penne rigate]].
Means knuckles; made with potatoes, semolina or wheat flour, and hard to pronounce from its spelling, which Jess used to read as 'noki'.
Origin unknown; theories include 'little turnips', though turnips were never part of it, and a word for a robe, though early ravioli could be unwrapped meatballs.
